derived: NVO turned 25.95% of revenue into free cash over 2023 to 2025 against the 49.5% its filed expense lines leave. Restated before interest: NVO paid 4,522mm DKK of interest inside operating cash flow over 2023 to 2025, 0.54% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so the charge falls by that much, from 29.59% to 29.04%. Restated at replacement capex: NVO spent 133,110mm DKK on plant over 2023 to 2025 against 19,625mm DKK of plant depreciation, 13.64% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge falls from 29.04% to 11.89%. Restated with selling costs: SG&A now carries NVO's filed selling or distribution costs, 20.81% of revenue this charge was absorbing, so it falls from 11.89% to nil. The filed lines alone now leave less than the cash the company made before interest and at replacement capex, and a charge below nil would credit the book with cash its own costs do not leave. Checked without one-off cash: deal payments are booked under investing, so free cash flow never carried them, and no settlement or transition tax is stated for the window, so the charge stands. Restated to the amortisation floor: the filed cost lines leave a 41.40% pre-tax margin where the cash over 2023 to 2025 supports 50.32%, so the charge rebuilds at -8.92%. It was held at nil, but NVO books 6,529mm DKK of non-cash amortisation of acquired intangibles inside its cost lines in FY2025 (0000353278-26-000012), 2.11% of revenue, so the charge stops at that floor: -2.11%. Restated without working capital build: over 2023 to 2025 NVO's cash flow statement shows receivables up 20,296mm DKK, inventories up 25,235mm DKK, payables up 15,158mm DKK, a working capital build of 30,373mm DKK, 3.65% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge was held at the amortisation floor, -2.11% where the filed figures rebuild it at -8.92%, and stays there.

ARTEMIS design, NCT06118281 (HRA research summary 4979, https://www.hra.nhs.uk/planning-and-improving-research/application-summaries/research-summaries/4979-artemis-ziltivekimab-vs-placebo-on-cvot-in-patients-with-acute-mi/; UC San Diego trial listing, https://clinicaltrials.ucsd.edu/trial/NCT06118281): a subcutaneous loading dose as early as possible after the invasive procedure and within 36 hours (STEMI) or 48 hours (NSTEMI) of admission, then once monthly, added to standard of care, over a treatment period estimated at up to 2 years. The trial is event-driven
column12: Monthly maintenance dosing, so chronic. Case against: the trial's own treatment period is about 2 years and the label may follow it. The discontinuation below gives a mean time on drug of about 2 years (1/0.505), close to that period, so a fixed course and a chronic line land in about the same place

column11: lookup.py demand Repatha: 'Repatha (3 presentations)', CMS Medicare Part D 2024, $1,962,120,377 over 459,932 beneficiaries = $4,266 per beneficiary
column12: Judgement on the comparator. Repatha is the closest marketed comparator in the same setting: a self-injected antibody, dosed every two weeks or monthly, used for secondary prevention after MI, and the largest by Medicare use. Case against: Praluent Pen, whose ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial enrolled patients after an acute coronary syndrome, reads lower at $3,683 (Part D 2024). Leqvio reads $6,135 on Part B. IL-6 antibodies priced for rheumatology read far higher: Kevzara $27,534 (Part D 2024) and Actemra $26,606 (Part D 2024). Novo would price for a mass cardiovascular population, not a rheumatology one. Per-beneficiary spend covers part-years, so it sits under an annual list price. Discrepancy to flag: the enlicitide seed quotes 'Repatha SureClick' at $4,470 ($1,709,589,708 over 382,461). The current drug_demand table has no such row, only 'Repatha (3 presentations)', which is used here. In DKK because the engine models a company in its reporting currency and converts to dollars only at the end: $4,266.00 at DKK/USD 0.152643 (ECB via fetchers/fx_ecb.py, 2026-09-23) is DKK 27,947.52

column12: First and recurrent heart attacks both count: ARTEMIS takes a prior MI as one of its qualifying risk criteria. About 1 in 5 are silent (same CDC page). eligible_pct removes those

column11: Two filters. (1) Hospitalised: 6,603,709 US AMI hospitalisations over 2004-2014 in the National Inpatient Sample (Matetic A et al., Am J Cardiol 2020;129:10-18, doi:10.1016/j.amjcard.2020.05.025, PMID 32576369), 600,337 a year, which is 0.7458 of the CDC 805,000. (2) Type 1 MI confirmed by invasive angiography, an ARTEMIS entry criterion: coronary angiography was done in 63.4% (lowest income quartile) to 64.3% (highest) of those hospitalisations (same paper). The midpoint, 0.6385, is used. 0.7458 x 0.6385 = 0.476, about 383,000 patients a year
column12: Judgement on the midpoint of the angiography range. Two further ARTEMIS criteria are not applied, because no source for their share was found: symptom onset within 12 hours (STEMI) or 24 hours (NSTEMI) before admission, and at least one risk enhancer (prior MI, prior revascularisation, treated diabetes, CKD, prior ischaemic stroke, carotid disease, PAD or multivessel disease). The enhancers are broad, but both filters cut the pool, so 0.476 is an upper bound on them. Case for lower: NIS counts admissions, so transfers between hospitals are counted twice, and AMI admissions have fallen since 2004-2014. Among NSTEMI admissions in 2016-2021 only 42.7% had angiography (Borovac JA et al., Cardiovasc Revasc Med 2025;75:98-104, doi:10.1016/j.carrev.2025.03.006), partly because ICD-10 codes type 2 MI as NSTEMI. Case for higher: a label may read 'adults with acute MI' without the angiography condition

column11: Incumbent: PCSK9 antibodies, the injectable add-on used for secondary prevention after MI. US starts within 1 year of an MI hospitalisation, July 2015-June 2020: 0.4% in Medicare, 0.4% in Optum CDM, 0.7% in MarketScan (Sloot R et al., Epidemiology 2024;35(4):579-588, doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001730, PMID 38629975). Weighted by the NSTEMI payer mix (Medicare 62.9%, other 37.1%; Vallabhajosyula 2021, as in discontinuation_pct): 0.511%. Updated to 2024 by the class's Medicare Part D beneficiaries (lookup.py demand): Repatha 111,259 plus Praluent Pen 52,834 = 164,093 in 2020, and 459,932 plus 92,483 = 552,415 in 2024, a 3.366x rise. 0.511% x 3.366 = 1.72%
column12: Judgement: the multiple over the updated PCSK9 rate is 1.0. Scaling by beneficiaries treats growth in the class's Medicare stock as growth in post-MI starts. With 50%+ annual discontinuation the stock settles within two to three years, so growth there mostly reflects higher starts. Scaling from 2020, the end of the study window, is conservative. The anchor is measured over all MI admissions, while the pool here is the angiography-confirmed subset, where PCSK9 users (younger, invasively managed) concentrate. Case for higher: ziltivekimab would be started in hospital at the index event with no LDL threshold to meet. A Japanese single-centre protocol lifted PCSK9 starts after AMI from 2.8% to 15.3% (Arai R et al., J Atheroscler Thromb 2025;32(11):1434-1446, doi:10.5551/jat.65731). Case for lower: ZEUS showed no MACE benefit (HR 0.99) despite full IL-6 and hsCRP suppression, and colchicine failed after MI in CLEAR SYNERGY, so cardiologists may doubt an anti-inflammatory even after a positive ARTEMIS. Payers will also meet a biologic in an 800,000-a-year population with the same restrictions they put on PCSK9s
